blocks.content: Tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies established to perform judicial or administrative functions and ensure speedy adjudication outside the traditional court hierarchy.

rows: Bound by strict provisions of the CPC and Indian Evidence Act
Guided flexibly by the Principles of Natural Justice
Includes both judicial and expert/technical members
Broad general jurisdiction over civil and criminal matters
Created under Article 323A or 323B by statute

items: Article 323A tribunals can be established ONLY by Parliament, whereas Article 323B tribunals can be established by BOTH Parliament and State Legislatures.
Post the L. Chandra Kumar Case (1997), appeals against tribunal decisions must go before a Division Bench of the concerned High Court before approaching the Supreme Court.
Tribunals consist of both judicial and technical members to provide domain expertise in technical matters.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies set up to adjudicate specific disputes and relieve overburdened traditional courts.
Part XIV-A was incorporated into the Constitution of India through the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, upon recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.
Article 323A provides for Administrative Tribunals for public service matters and can be created solely by Parliament.
Article 323B enables both Parliament and State Legislatures to establish tribunals for subjects like taxation, land reforms, and foreign exchange.
Unlike ordinary courts, tribunals are guided by the Principles of Natural Justice rather than strict procedural codes like the CPC or Indian Evidence Act.
